\section{Introduction}

Many directed networks are assembled from modules. A base graph describes interactions among communities, while each community has its own internal directed structure. The generalized join models an especially symmetric architecture: if the base contains an arc from community $i$ to community $j$, every vertex in the first community is connected to every vertex in the second. Weighted arcs permit the common coupling strength to vary with the ordered pair of communities.

The construction is combinatorially large but algebraically structured. If fiber $i$ has $n_i$ vertices, one base arc can expand into $n_in_j$ directed arcs. Direct work with the full Laplacian can obscure the smaller ingredients from which it was built. Our purpose is to expose those ingredients through a canonical invariant splitting.

There are two natural kinds of network signals. A signal may fluctuate internally while having zero total in every fiber, or it may be constant inside each fiber and vary only at base level. Complete bipartite coupling reacts only to fiber totals. Zero-mass fluctuations are therefore invisible to cross-fiber coupling, whereas fiber-constant signals reduce exactly to a weighted quotient action.

This splitting is the spectral mechanism needed in generalized-join spanning-tree calculations. The directed matrix-tree theorem converts rooted arborescence counts into reduced Laplacian determinants. Once a Laplacian separates into local fluctuation blocks and a global quotient block, determinant factors can be associated with internal spectra and quotient data. We establish the operator-theoretic foundation. A final rooted-tree formula additionally requires a fixed orientation convention and an analysis of reduced determinants.

The basic identities hold over any commutative ring. The direct-sum construction requires division by fiber cardinalities and is stated over a characteristic-zero field with nonempty fibers.

\section{Generalized joins and Laplacian action}

Let $I$ be a finite index set. For each $i\in I$, let $H_i$ be a finite digraph with vertex set $V_i$ and size $n_i=|V_i|$. Let $A=(A_{ij})$ be a matrix over a commutative ring $R$. The entry $A_{ij}$ is the weight assigned to every external arc from a vertex of $V_i$ to a vertex of $V_j$. Thus a weighted base arc $i\to j$ becomes a complete directed bipartite family of arcs $u\to v$, with $u\in V_i$ and $v\in V_j$.

For each $i$, let $L_i$ be a linear operator on functions $V_i\to R$. A fibered vector is a collection $x=(x_i)_{i\in I}$ with $x_i:V_i\to R$.

\begin{definition}[Fiber mass and external degree]
The mass of $x$ in fiber $i$ and the weighted external out-degree at fiber $i$ are
\[
m_i(x)=\sum_{u\in V_i}x_i(u),
\qquad
d_i=\sum_{j\in I}A_{ij}n_j.
\]
\end{definition}

The factor $n_j$ appears because each source vertex in $V_i$ has $n_j$ possible destinations in $V_j$.

\begin{definition}[Generalized-join Laplacian]
The generalized-join operator $\mathcal L$ is
\[
(\mathcal Lx)_i(u)=(L_ix_i)(u)+d_ix_i(u)-\sum_{j\in I}A_{ij}m_j(x).
\]
\end{definition}

The terms represent internal action, external diagonal degree, and complete-bipartite coupling to fiber masses. When the $L_i$ are internal out-Laplacians, this is the out-Laplacian action of the generalized join.

\begin{definition}[Fiber-constant lift and quotient]
For $z:I\to R$, define $(Cz)_i(u)=z_i$. Define the quotient operator $Q$ by
\[
(Qz)_i=d_iz_i-\sum_{j\in I}A_{ij}n_jz_j.
\]
If $N=\diag(n_i)$ and $D=\diag(d_i)$, then $Q=D-AN$.
\end{definition}

The destination-size matrix $N$ is essential: the quotient is generally not $D-A$.

\section{The zero-mass sector}

Let
\[
Z=\{x:m_i(x)=0\text{ for every }i\in I\}.
\]

\begin{theorem}[Zero-mass decoupling]
If $x\in Z$, then
\[
(\mathcal Lx)_i(u)=(L_ix_i)(u)+d_ix_i(u)
\]
for every $i$ and $u\in V_i$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
The inter-fiber term is $\sum_jA_{ij}m_j(x)$, and each mass is zero.
\end{proof}

Complete bipartite coupling thus communicates only aggregate mass. Balanced variations inside a fiber cannot be detected by other fibers.

\begin{theorem}[Assembled shifted eigenvector]
Let $\rho\in R$. Suppose $x\in Z$ and
\[
(L_ix_i)(u)=(\rho-d_i)x_i(u)
\]
for every $i$ and $u\in V_i$. Then $\mathcal Lx=\rho x$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Zero-mass decoupling gives
\[
(\mathcal Lx)_i(u)=(\rho-d_i)x_i(u)+d_ix_i(u)=\rho x_i(u).
\]
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Supported-fiber eigenvalue shift]
Fix $i_0\in I$. Suppose $x_j=0$ for $j\ne i_0$, the component $x_{i_0}$ has zero mass, every internal operator satisfies $L_j0=0$, and
\[
L_{i_0}x_{i_0}=\mu x_{i_0}.
\]
Then
\[
\mathcal Lx=(\mu+d_{i_0})x.
\]
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
All fiber masses vanish. In the active fiber, zero-mass decoupling gives $(\mu+d_{i_0})x_{i_0}$. In every inactive fiber, both the vector and its internal image vanish.
\end{proof}

Thus every zero-mass internal eigenvalue $\mu$ in fiber $i$ contributes the shifted value $\mu+d_i$ to the full operator.

\begin{assumption}[Internal mass preservation]
For every $i$ and every $y:V_i\to R$,
\[
\sum_{u\in V_i}y(u)=0
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\sum_{u\in V_i}(L_iy)(u)=0.
\]
\end{assumption}

\begin{theorem}[Zero-mass invariance]
Under internal mass preservation, $x\in Z$ implies $\mathcal Lx\in Z$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
By decoupling,
\[
\sum_{u\in V_i}(\mathcal Lx)_i(u)
=\sum_{u\in V_i}(L_ix_i)(u)+d_i\sum_{u\in V_i}x_i(u)=0.
\]
The first term vanishes by mass preservation and the second by $x\in Z$.
\end{proof}

\section{Fiber constants and quotient dynamics}

Let $\mathcal C=\{Cz:z\in R^I\}$.

\begin{assumption}[Constants in the internal kernel]
For every $i$ and scalar $c\in R$,
\[
L_i(c\mathbf 1_{V_i})=0.
\]
\end{assumption}

\begin{theorem}[Fiber-constant intertwining]
Under the constant-kernel assumption, every base vector $z$ satisfies
\[
\mathcal L(Cz)=C(Qz).
\]
Consequently, $\mathcal C$ is invariant under $\mathcal L$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
The lift has mass $n_jz_j$ in fiber $j$, and its internal action vanishes. Hence
\[
(\mathcal L(Cz))_i(u)=d_iz_i-\sum_jA_{ij}n_jz_j=(Qz)_i,
\]
independent of $u$.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Lifting quotient eigenvectors]
If $Qz=\rho z$, then $\mathcal L(Cz)=\rho Cz$.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Use the intertwining identity and linearity of $C$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Constant modes]
The all-ones base vector satisfies $Q\mathbf 1=0$. Under the constant-kernel assumption, the global all-ones vector also satisfies $\mathcal L\mathbf 1=0$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
For each $i$,
\[
(Q\mathbf 1)_i=d_i-\sum_jA_{ij}n_j=0
\]
by the definition of $d_i$. The full-network statement follows by lifting.
\end{proof}

The quotient weights depend asymmetrically on destination sizes. Even if $A$ is symmetric, $Q$ can be nonsymmetric when fiber sizes differ.

\section{Canonical direct-sum decomposition}

Let $K$ be a characteristic-zero field, and suppose every $V_i$ is nonempty. Then the positive integer $n_i$ is nonzero in $K$ and hence invertible.

\begin{definition}[Average and centering]
For a fibered vector $x$, define
\[
\bar x_i=\frac{m_i(x)}{n_i},
\qquad
x_i^{\circ}(u)=x_i(u)-\bar x_i.
\]
The vectors $x^{\circ}$ and $C\bar x$ are respectively the centered fluctuation and fiber-average components.
\end{definition}

\begin{lemma}[Centered mass]
For every $i$, $m_i(x^{\circ})=0$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Summing over $V_i$ gives
\[
m_i(x^{\circ})=m_i(x)-n_i\bar x_i
=m_i(x)-n_i\frac{m_i(x)}{n_i}=0.
\]
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Reconstruction]
Every vector satisfies $x=x^{\circ}+C\bar x$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
At coordinate $(i,u)$, the right side is $x_i(u)-\bar x_i+\bar x_i=x_i(u)$.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Trivial intersection]
If $Cz$ has zero mass in every fiber, then $Cz=0$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
The mass in fiber $i$ is $n_iz_i$. Since $n_i\ne0$ in $K$, zero mass implies $z_i=0$ for every $i$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Canonical direct sum]
Over a characteristic-zero field with nonempty fibers,
\[
K^{\bigsqcup_iV_i}=Z\oplus\mathcal C.
\]
The unique decomposition is $x=x^{\circ}+C\bar x$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Centered mass and reconstruction prove existence. The trivial-intersection lemma proves uniqueness.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Invariant two-scale splitting]
If internal operators preserve zero mass and kill constants, then both summands are invariant. Explicitly,
\[
\mathcal Lx^{\circ}\in Z,
\qquad
\mathcal L(C\bar x)=C(Q\bar x).
\]
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Apply zero-mass invariance to the centered component and fiber-constant intertwining to the average component.
\end{proof}

In a basis adapted to this direct sum,
\[
\mathcal L\sim
\left(\bigoplus_{i\in I}(L_i+d_iI)\big|_{Z_i}\right)\oplus Q,
\quad
Z_i=\left\{y:V_i\to K:\sum_{u\in V_i}y(u)=0\right\}.
\]
This block interpretation explains both local eigenvalue shifts and quotient eigenvector lifts.

\section{Algorithms}

\subsection{Implicit application}

The full dense matrix need not be formed. Compute every mass $m_j$, every degree $d_i$, and every coupling scalar $c_i=\sum_jA_{ij}m_j$. Return
\[
(L_ix_i)(u)+d_ix_i(u)-c_i
\]
at each coordinate. If internal actions cost $T_i$, dense base weights require
\[
O\!\left(\sum_iT_i+|I|^2+\sum_in_i\right)
\]
arithmetic operations. Sparse base weights replace $|I|^2$ by the number of nonzero base arcs.

\subsection{Two-scale projection}

For each fiber, compute $\bar x_i=n_i^{-1}\sum_ux_i(u)$ and set $x_i^{\circ}(u)=x_i(u)-\bar x_i$. The cost is $O(\sum_in_i)$, and reconstruction is coordinatewise addition.

\subsection{Spectral assembly}

Compute $d_i$ and $Q=D-AN$. For each zero-mass internal eigenpair $(\mu,y)$ of $L_i$, extend $y$ by zero and assign eigenvalue $\mu+d_i$. Compute eigenpairs $(\rho,z)$ of $Q$ and lift $z$. If local and quotient eigenvectors are complete, their union is an eigenbasis. Dense numerical eigensolvers then cost approximately
\[
O\!\left(\sum_in_i^3+|I|^3\right)
\]
rather than $O((\sum_in_i)^3)$. For defective operators one should retain invariant blocks or generalized eigenvectors rather than assert an eigenbasis.

\section{Numerical examples}

\subsection{Two bidirectionally joined fibers}

Take fiber sizes $n_1=2$, $n_2=3$ and
\[
A=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}.
\]
Then $d_1=3$, $d_2=2$, and
\[
Q=\begin{pmatrix}3&-3\\-2&2\end{pmatrix}.
\]
Its eigenvalues are $0$ and $5$. The zero mode is $(1,1)$; an eigenvector for $5$ is $(3,-2)$.

Choose internal Laplacians
\[
L_1=\begin{pmatrix}1&-1\\-1&1\end{pmatrix},
\qquad
L_2=\begin{pmatrix}2&-1&-1\\-1&2&-1\\-1&-1&2\end{pmatrix}.
\]
The first has zero-mass eigenvalue $2$, shifted to $2+3=5$. The second has two zero-mass eigenvalues equal to $3$, shifted to $3+2=5$. Hence the full five-vertex operator has eigenvalues
\[
0,5,5,5,5.
\]
One coarse mode, one local mode from the first fiber, and two local modes from the second coincide at $5$.

\subsection{A weighted asymmetric base}

Let the sizes be $(2,1,3)$ and
\[
A=\begin{pmatrix}0&2&0\\1&0&1\\3&0&0\end{pmatrix}.
\]
Then $(d_1,d_2,d_3)=(2,5,6)$ and
\[
Q=\begin{pmatrix}2&-2&0\\-2&5&-3\\-6&0&6\end{pmatrix}.
\]
Every row sums to zero, despite unequal sizes and asymmetric coupling. Fiber-constant signals evolve exactly under this $3\times3$ matrix; centered components evolve under shifted internal operators.

\subsection{Full block-matrix check}

The diagonal block for fiber $i$ is $L_i+d_iI$. The block from input fiber $j$ to output fiber $i$ is
\[
-A_{ij}\mathbf 1_{n_i}\mathbf 1_{n_j}^{\mathsf T}
\]
for $i\ne j$, with the same coupling contribution included when diagonal base weights are permitted. Numerical comparison verifies that its spectrum is the union of shifted zero-mass internal spectra and the quotient spectrum under the decomposition hypotheses.

\section{Directed spanning trees}

A rooted directed spanning tree, or arborescence, is a spanning subgraph with a designated root and a unique directed connectivity pattern relative to it. Arcs may point toward or away from the root; the corresponding matrix-tree theorem uses a reduced determinant whose row-versus-column convention must match that orientation.

The invariant splitting contributes at determinant level. On the zero-mass sector, the blocks are shifted internal operators. On the fiber-constant sector, the block is $Q$. In an adapted basis, determinants of suitable restrictions factor into products of local shifted factors and quotient factors.

A reduced Laplacian, however, deletes a root row and column and is not simply the unrestricted operator. Deriving total arborescence counts or counts with the root restricted to one fiber requires proving how root deletion interacts with the split, or using an equivalent determinant transformation. A biclique-directed-star transformation may provide such a route by replacing a complete directed bipartite coupling with an auxiliary star while preserving the relevant reduced determinant. No such transformation is assumed here.

The established conclusions are therefore exact but bounded: the full action has the displayed formula; zero-mass modes acquire external-degree shifts; fiber constants are governed by $Q$; and the two sectors form an invariant direct sum under the stated hypotheses. These facts supply the spectral mechanism needed before the matrix-tree theorem is applied.

\section{Applications and discussion}

\paragraph{Community-structured analysis.}
The direct sum separates within-community contrasts from between-community averages. Spectral filters preserve this split when defined from $\mathcal L$: local filtering uses shifted internal spectra, while coarse filtering uses $Q$.

\paragraph{Graph coarsening and hierarchical learning.}
Pooling node features to fiber averages is exact for generalized-join coupling, not heuristic. The average sector is invariant and represented exactly by the quotient; the centered residual is invariant under mass preservation. This gives a solvable benchmark for hierarchical message passing and deviations from equitable block structure.

\paragraph{Diffusion and consensus.}
For $\dot x=-\mathcal Lx$, centered and coarse components evolve independently. Local rates are shifted by $d_i$, inter-fiber consensus is controlled by $Q$, and the global constant mode is stationary. In nonsymmetric settings, stability also depends on Jordan structure, but the invariant split persists.

\paragraph{Computation.}
The decomposition avoids constructing a dense matrix on all vertices. If internal spectra are known, only the small quotient requires new global analysis.

The distinction between ring-level identities and field-level decomposition is important. In positive characteristic, a fiber size may become zero as a scalar. Then a nonzero fiber-constant vector can have zero fiber mass, and the direct-sum theorem may fail even though decoupling and intertwining remain valid. Likewise, killing constants and preserving zero mass are separate assumptions, corresponding to different sum conventions for directed Laplacians.

\section{Future directions}

Natural next steps are to identify the abstract action with finite weighted out-Laplacian matrices; develop rooted in- and out-arborescences with a fixed orientation convention; factor reduced determinants using the invariant split; derive total and fiber-restricted spanning-tree formulas; prove a biclique-directed-star transformation as both a determinant and counting identity; and extend the weighted model to parallel arcs before specializing to unweighted simple digraphs.

For applications, exact complete bipartite coupling is an idealization. Perturbation theory for nearly constant inter-fiber blocks could bound leakage between centered and coarse sectors and quantify the reliability of graph coarsening and community-level learning.

\section{Conclusion}

The Laplacian of a weighted generalized join has a canonical two-scale organization. Complete bipartite coupling sees only fiber masses. Fiberwise zero-mass modes therefore decouple and acquire external-degree shifts, while fiber-constant modes evolve through $Q=D-AN$. Over a characteristic-zero field with nonempty fibers, centering and averaging uniquely decompose every signal. Under standard Laplacian hypotheses, both summands are invariant.

This structure clarifies spectrum, supports efficient computation, and prepares determinant factorizations for directed spanning-tree enumeration. A network made of networks is thereby resolved into local fluctuations and global flow.

    return [[float(size - 1 if i == j else -1) for j in range(size)] for i in range(size)]

        return [len(block) for block in self.internal]

    def external_degrees(self) -> Vector:
        return matvec(self.base_weights, self.sizes)

        degrees = self.external_degrees()

        masses = [sum(fiber) for fiber in fibers]

        couplings = matvec(self.base_weights, masses)
        return [

Vector = list[float]
Matrix = list[list[float]]


def matvec(matrix: Matrix, vector: Sequence[float]) -> Vector:
    """Multiply a rectangular matrix by a vector."""
    return [sum(a * b for a, b in zip(row, vector)) for row in matrix]


def add_vectors(left: Sequence[float], right: Sequence[float]) -> Vector:
    return [a + b for a, b in zip(left, right)]


def scale(scalar: float, vector: Sequence[float]) -> Vector:

def max_error(left: Sequence[float], right: Sequence[float]) -> float:

def assert_close(left: Sequence[float], right: Sequence[float], tolerance: float = 1e-9) -> None:

    if size <= 0:
        raise ValueError("size must be positive")

        couplings = matvec(self.base_weights, masses)
        return [
            [internal_value + degrees[i] * value - couplings[i]

    def split(self, fibers: Sequence[Sequence[float]]) -> tuple[list[Vector], Vector]:

concept.concept_description: An Escher staircase is an infinite strictly ascending chain of ideals I_1 strictly contained in I_2 strictly contained in ... that nevertheless has I_1 as an element of the infinite intersection. This seems impossible — how can an infinite ascending chain loop back to the beginning? But in the ring of integer-valued polynomials Int(Z), the chain I_n = {f in Int(Z) : f(Z) contained in 2^n Z} is strictly ascending (I_n strictly contained in I_{n+1}) yet the intersection of all I_n is {0}, which contains the zero polynomial that is also in I_1. Conjecture: Every non-Noetherian ring contains an Escher staircase, and the 'height' of the Escher effect (measured by the Krull dimension gap) is a new ring invariant. For Int(Z), the Escher height is infinite (the chain never stabilizes). For Z[x_1, x_2, ...], the Escher height equals the number of variables. For the p-adic integers Z_p, there is NO Escher staircase (Z_p is a DVR, hence Noetherian). Test: prove that Int(Z) has an Escher staircase of infinite height. Prove that k[x_1,...,x_n] has Escher height n. Compute the Escher height for the ring of all algebraic integers. Impact: a new invariant for non-Noetherian rings that measures how far a ring is from being Noetherian — the algebraic equivalent of Escher's impossible architecture.
